home.problem.title: Every session is day one. Until now.
home.problem.p1: You explain the project again. You restate the rule you set last week. The agent rediscovers the bug it already fixed. Context windows end, and everything in them ends with them.
home.problem.p2: CortexMind is the part of the stack that was missing: a memory that outlives the conversation, read before the agent plans and written before it stops.

home.how.title: Three steps, then it just runs.
home.how.lead: Install once. Your agents boot with memory from the next conversation on.
home.how.step1.title: Install and paste your key
home.how.step1.body: Download the app for macOS, Windows or Linux and paste the license key from your receipt. The app lives in your tray and runs the memory daemon in the background.
home.how.step2.title: Connect your agent
home.how.step2.body: Copy one config snippet from the tray menu into Claude Code, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, Codex or Cursor. Local agents talk to it on localhost. claude.ai and other hosted agents reach it through the bundled hosted tunnel.
home.how.step2_link: Connect ChatGPT or Claude on the web
home.how.step3.title: Every conversation starts with memory
home.how.step3.body: The agent boots with your standing rules and the last turns, searches memory as the topic moves, and saves the turn before it ends. You stop repeating yourself.
home.retrieval.title: Finds what you meant, not what you typed.
home.retrieval.p1: Keyword search and semantic search run side by side and get fused. A cross-encoder then reranks the candidates and lands on the exact passage inside a long note. The importance you set and the age of a memory settle the ties.
home.retrieval.p2: No language model sits in the write path. What you save is what gets stored, in full, on your disk.

home.retrieval.hit1_text: Staging stays on the shared Postgres until the migration lands. Nobody runs the prod-to-dev copy as a test.
home.retrieval.hit2_text: The prod-to-dev migration is manual only. Mat runs it, never an agent.

home.boot.title: Starts every conversation already knowing your rules.
home.boot.p1: The boot call returns your standing rules, the preferences and conventions you promoted to the top, plus where the last conversation left off. The agent has them before you type a word.
home.boot.p2: When the card grows too long, CortexMind tells the agent to ask you to prune it. Your memory stays sharp instead of piling up.

home.boot.rule3: Tests run in the container, never on the host

home.local.title: Yours. On your machine.
home.local.col1.title: Local first
home.local.col1.body: Memories live in one SQLite file in your home directory. No account, no cloud sync, no telemetry on your content. Back it up like any other file.
home.local.col2.title: Any GPU, or none
home.local.col2.body: Apple Silicon runs the models on Metal. NVIDIA, AMD and Intel cards run them on Vulkan. No graphics card runs them on the CPU, slower and still correct. Nothing to configure.

home.requirements.title: What it needs
home.requirements.cpu_val: Any 64-bit CPU. 6 cores or more recommended without a GPU
home.requirements.gpu_val: Optional. Apple Silicon (Metal) or any Vulkan-capable GPU: NVIDIA, AMD, Intel Arc. About 2 GB of GPU memory in use; an 8 GB card is more than enough
home.requirements.disk_val: 10 GB free. The models take about 3 GB, downloaded once
home.requirements.os_val: macOS 11 or newer on Apple Silicon, Windows 10 or 11, Linux with glibc 2.39 or newer
home.requirements.note: Without a graphics card the models run on the CPU and everything still works. With one, CortexMind times your CPU against every GPU it can see on first launch and keeps the fastest.
home.faq.title: Questions
home.faq.q1: Do I need a graphics card?
home.faq.a1: No. The embedding and reranking models run on the CPU when nothing else is available. A GPU makes saving and recall faster on a large memory, and CortexMind picks it up on its own: Metal on Apple Silicon, Vulkan on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel cards.
home.faq.a2: In one SQLite database in your home directory. You can back it up, copy it to another machine or delete it like any file. Nothing is synced to a server.
home.faq.a3: Any client that speaks MCP. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, claude.ai, ChatGPT, Codex and Cursor are the ones the tray menu has ready-made snippets for.
home.faq.q4: How does the agent know when to remember?
home.faq.a4: The tools carry their own instructions: boot with memory_init, search as the topic moves, save before the turn ends. A short block in your CLAUDE.md or system prompt turns that into a habit. The docs page has the block to paste.
home.faq.q5: Can several agents share one memory?
home.faq.a5: Yes, that is the point. One daemon on your machine serves every client you connect, so what one agent learns the next one knows.
home.faq.a6: The app keeps working until the end of the paid period, plus a 72-hour offline grace. Your database stays on disk untouched. Subscribe again and everything is back.
home.faq.a7: The license check talks to Polar. If you turn on the hosted tunnel, requests from hosted agents pass through the relay to your machine over HTTPS. Your memories are never uploaded anywhere.
home.faq.a8: The monthly plan starts with a 14-day trial so you can decide before paying anything. For anything else, write to info@cortexmind.net.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.lead: From download to an agent that remembers, in about ten minutes. Most of it is waiting for the models to download.
docs.install.title: Install
docs.install.p1: Download the build for your platform and open it. CortexMind installs like any desktop app and then lives in your system tray.
docs.install.mac: macOS: open the DMG and drag CortexMind to Applications. Apple Silicon only.
docs.install.windows: Windows: run the installer. The Visual C++ runtime is bundled.
docs.install.linux: Linux: make the AppImage executable and run it.
docs.install.p2: On first launch, paste the license key from your receipt. It looks like this:
docs.install.p3: The app then downloads the two models it needs, about three gigabytes. A progress bar shows the download. Once it says ready, the memory daemon is running and will start with your session from now on.
docs.connect.title: Connect an agent
docs.connect.web_callout: Using ChatGPT or Claude on the web, phone or desktop app? Follow the step-by-step guide.
docs.connect.p1: CortexMind is an MCP server on your machine. Local agents reach it at this address with a bearer token the app generated for you. The tray menu has a Connect page with the snippet already filled in, so you never type the token by hand.
docs.connect.claude_code_p: One command in your terminal. Paste the token from the Connect page where it says token.
docs.connect.cursor_p: Add the server to .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or to the global file in your home directory.
docs.connect.codex_p: Codex reads its servers from config.toml, including the one in the ChatGPT desktop app. Put the token in the Authorization header, as below.
docs.connect.hosted_p: Hosted agents cannot reach localhost. Turn on the hosted tunnel in the app and add the tunnel address as a custom connector. They sign in with OAuth, no token to paste. See remote access below.
docs.connect.p2: Any other client that speaks MCP over HTTP works the same way: the address, plus the Authorization header.
docs.protocol.title: Teach it to remember
docs.protocol.p1: The tools describe themselves, and most agents will use them once connected. To make memory a habit rather than a hope, add a short standing instruction where your agent reads its rules: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, the project instructions in claude.ai, custom instructions in ChatGPT, AGENTS.md for Codex, rules in Cursor.
docs.protocol.p2: The full protocol ships inside the app, on the Connect page. This is the part that matters:
docs.protocol.block:
## Memory

Use CortexMind as my only memory. Ignore any built-in memory feature; it was migrated into CortexMind and is switched off.

FIRST action of every conversation: `memory_init()`, then `memory_search("<topic of the request>")`.

`memory_init` returns the titles of my standing rules plus recent continuity. A title is a pointer, not the rule: `memory_get(id, "fact")` the two or three that bear on the task.

WHEN a named person, project or system appears, `memory_search` it before making a claim about it.
WHEN the topic shifts, search again.
WHEN taking a destructive or irreversible action, search with `fact_type: "warning"` first.

LAST action of every response: `memory_save(user_request=..., agent_response=...)`. Write both for a reader months from now. Bump `importance` to 8 or more for identity, family and lifelong preferences. Durable claims also get `memory_save_fact`.

Without the save, the conversation is lost.
docs.protocol.p3: Standing rules, the preferences and conventions you want in every conversation, belong in memory, not in this file. Save them as facts of type preference or convention at importance eight or higher and memory_init delivers them at every boot.
docs.seed.title: Seed your memory
docs.seed.p1: A memory that starts empty takes a week to become useful. The app ships an interview prompt that skips that week: paste it into your agent, and it will check the connection, then ask about who you are, who you work with, what you are building and how you like things done, saving as you go.
docs.seed.p2: Find it on the Connect page of the app, under Seed my memory. Run it once, in the agent you use most.
docs.remote.title: Remote access
docs.remote.p1: Your license includes a hosted tunnel. Turn it on in the app and your memory becomes reachable at an address of the form
docs.remote.p2: claude.ai: Settings, Connectors, Add custom connector, paste the address. claude.ai signs in with OAuth and asks you to approve it once. ChatGPT works the same way from its connector settings. Claude Desktop uses the same connector list as claude.ai.
docs.remote.p3: The tunnel forwards requests to the daemon on your machine over HTTPS. Turn it off and the address stops answering. One license activates one machine on the tunnel.
docs.tools.title: The tools
docs.tools.lead: Eleven tools, each with instructions the agent reads. The names are the vocabulary your agent will use when it talks about its memory.
docs.tools.d_init: The first call of every conversation. Returns standing rules as titles plus ids, and the last few turns for continuity.
docs.tools.d_search: Search long-term memory by meaning and keyword. Every hit carries a score; 0.7 and up is strong.
docs.tools.d_recall: Walk the episode timeline, newest first, with no query. Bound it with since and until.
docs.tools.d_get: Fetch one full record by id when the search excerpt was not enough.
docs.tools.d_save: Save the turn at the end of every response. The only write path.
docs.tools.d_save_fact: Pin a durable claim as its own record, separate from the turn that produced it.
docs.tools.d_status: Counts, model state and health of the daemon.
docs.tools.d_archive: Retire noise that needs no replacement. Requires a reason, audit-logged.
docs.tools.d_supersede: Replace a stale record with a corrected one, keeping a forward link.
docs.tools.d_set_importance: Re-rank a record. Drop a standing rule to 7 to take it off the boot card without losing it.
docs.tools.d_ack: Snooze the boot card pruning nudge after you and your agent reviewed it.
docs.data.title: Your data
docs.data.p1: Everything lives in one folder in your home directory:
docs.data.db: memory.db is a SQLite database with your episodes, facts and their embeddings.
docs.data.config: config.toml holds the ports, the bearer token, the tunnel setting and the accelerator choice.
docs.data.models: The models sit next to them, about three gigabytes, downloaded once.
docs.data.p2: To back up, quit CortexMind and copy the folder. To move to a new machine, install there, restore the folder, activate with your key. Nothing on our side holds a copy.
docs.troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
docs.troubleshooting.q1: The agent does not see any memory tools
docs.troubleshooting.a1: Check that CortexMind shows ready in the tray, that the address in your config is http://localhost:14200/mcp, and that the Authorization header carries the token from the Connect page. Restart the agent after editing its config.
docs.troubleshooting.a2: Add the standing instruction above to the file your agent reads at startup. Without it, saving depends on the agent's mood.
docs.troubleshooting.a3: The models are about three gigabytes and download once. The app shows the progress. On a slow connection this can take a while; leave it running.
docs.troubleshooting.a4: The app re-checks your key every hour and keeps working for 72 hours without a connection. If the subscription lapsed, renew it in your customer portal and the app picks it up within the hour.
docs.troubleshooting.a5: On a machine without a GPU, search on a large memory takes a couple of seconds. Apple Silicon and Vulkan GPUs are picked up automatically. Check the accelerator line in the app's status.
docs.uninstall.title: Uninstall
docs.uninstall.p1: Quit the app from the tray, remove it like any application, and delete the folder in your home directory if you want the memory gone too. Cancel the subscription from your customer portal.

privacy.meta.description: What CortexMind collects, which is almost nothing.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.s1: CortexMind stores your memories in a database on your computer. The application never uploads them. There is no server that receives, stores or reads memory content, and nobody but you can access the database on your machine.
privacy.s2: The app sends your license key to Polar, our merchant of record, about once an hour, to confirm the subscription is active. The auto-updater fetches a small manifest from GitHub to learn whether a new version exists. Neither request carries memory content.
privacy.s3: If you turn on the hosted tunnel, requests from hosted agents such as claude.ai pass through a relay operated for CortexMind on their way to your machine, over HTTPS. The relay routes traffic; it does not store memories. Turn the tunnel off and nothing passes through it.
privacy.s4: Checkout, payment, invoices and the customer portal are run by Polar. Polar collects your email address and payment details under its own privacy policy. We see your email address and the status of your subscription, nothing about your card.
privacy.s5: cortexmind.net is served by Cloudflare Pages. It sets no analytics cookies and runs no tracking scripts. Your theme and language choices are kept in your browser only.
privacy.s6: Questions about privacy go to info@cortexmind.net.

docs.ai.title: Let your AI install it
docs.ai.lead: The fastest path. One prompt, pasted into an agent that can run commands on your machine: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor in agent mode, or any other agentic AI.
docs.ai.p1: Buy first: the prompt asks for your license key, and it tells you how the key is handled before asking. Your AI then finds the right build on this site, installs it, waits for the models, reads the access token the app generated, registers CortexMind as its own MCP server, and adds the memory habit to its instructions. It then migrates the memories it already keeps, in files or in a built-in memory feature, into CortexMind, asks you to switch that built-in memory off, and interviews you to seed the rest. If the agent needs a restart to load the new server, paste the same prompt again and it picks up where it stopped.
docs.ai.manual: Prefer to do it by hand? The manual steps follow.
docs.manual.title: Manual install
home.how.ai_title: Or let your AI do all three.
home.how.ai_body: One prompt pasted into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent with a shell installs the app, connects the agent, moves the memories it already keeps into CortexMind, and interviews you to seed the rest.
home.pricing.fine_pre: One license activates one machine. Tax is handled at checkout by Polar, the merchant of record. Your license key lives in your
docs.ai.model_note: Use your strongest model for the setup: in ChatGPT or Codex, a GPT-6 model such as Astra; in Claude, Sonnet 5 or Opus 5.5. Smaller models tend to improvise. You can switch back afterwards.
home.faq.q9: What about the memory my AI already has?
home.faq.a9: The setup prompt has the agent read through whatever it already remembers, memory files on disk or a built-in memory feature, and save each durable fact into CortexMind. Once that is done it asks you to switch the built-in memory off, so there is one memory, not two competing ones.
home.faq.q10: Does my computer need to stay on?
home.faq.a10: Only while you want the memory available. For most people CortexMind runs on the computer they are working on and starts with the session, so there is nothing to think about. If you want claude.ai, ChatGPT or the phone apps to reach your memory at any hour, the machine running CortexMind has to be on and reachable at that moment: leave a home computer running, or install CortexMind on a small VPS in the cloud so it is always online.
home.faq.q11: How do web and phone apps reach it?
home.faq.a11: Through the hosted tunnel. Turn it on in the app and CortexMind gets an HTTPS address that claude.ai, ChatGPT or any remote MCP client can add as a connector, signing in with OAuth. The tunnel is EtherTunnel, a separate product: your CortexMind license includes a free EtherTunnel license with one tunnel.
home.compound.title: Your AI gets better every week.
home.compound.lead: With a real memory, the model matters less and what it knows about you matters more. Every conversation leaves it a little sharper, and the improvement compounds.
home.compound.col1.title: Tell it, and it is a rule
home.compound.col1.body: No instructions file to edit, no prompt to rewrite. Say "remember that I want PR descriptions under 100 words" and it is a standing rule from the next conversation on.
home.compound.col2.title: The model matters less
home.compound.col2.body: Switch models, switch tools, keep the memory. What makes your agent good is what it has accumulated about you and your work, and that stays yours.
home.compound.col3.title: Send it to learn
home.compound.col3.body: Point it at a topic, a codebase or a pile of documents and let it read. What it saves is there for every agent, every conversation, from then on.

connect.meta.title: Connect ChatGPT and Claude to CortexMind
connect.meta.description: Step by step: add your CortexMind memory to ChatGPT and Claude on the web, then use it on your phone and in their desktop apps.
connect.title: Connect ChatGPT and Claude
connect.lead: CortexMind runs on your computer. ChatGPT and Claude reach it through your CortexMind's private web address. Set it up once per service and it follows you wherever you are signed in: the website, the phone app and the desktop app.
connect.before.title: Before you start
connect.before.running: CortexMind is running: the brain icon in your menu bar or system tray says Running.
connect.before.values: Open CortexMind's Settings. Under “Your CortexMind Endpoint” you will copy two values: the Public URL (it looks like https://cm-xxxxxxxxxxxx.ethertunnel.com/mcp) and the CortexMind Password.
connect.before.awake: Keep that computer on. When it sleeps, ChatGPT and Claude cannot reach your memory.
connect.chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
connect.chatgpt.plans: Needs a paid plan: Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise or Edu. On a Business or Enterprise workspace, an admin may have to allow custom connectors first.
connect.chatgpt.s1: On chatgpt.com, click your name at the bottom left, then Settings.
connect.chatgpt.s2: Open Apps (it may be called Plugins or Connectors). Scroll to the bottom, open Advanced settings and turn on Developer mode. ChatGPT warns that this allows unverified connectors: that is expected, CortexMind is your own server.
connect.chatgpt.s3: Close that window. A + button (Create) now appears next to the list of apps. Click it.
connect.chatgpt.s4: Name: CortexMind. Description: optional, for example “My long-term memory”. MCP server URL: paste your Public URL.
connect.chatgpt.s5: Authentication: choose Access token / API key, type Bearer. Tick “I understand and want to continue”, then click Create.
connect.chatgpt.s6: When ChatGPT asks for the access token or API key, paste your CortexMind Password and save.
connect.chatgpt.s7: Teach it the habit: in Settings, open Personalization, then Custom instructions. Paste the AI Instructions from CortexMind's Settings (Copy button, English or French) and save.
connect.chatgpt.s8: Test it: start a new chat and ask “What do you know about me?”. The first time, ChatGPT asks permission to use CortexMind: allow it. If it answers without checking your memory, click + in the message box and make sure CortexMind is turned on.
connect.claude.title: Claude
connect.claude.plans: Works on every plan. The Free plan allows one custom connector; Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise allow more.
connect.claude.s1: On claude.ai, open Customize, then Connectors. On older layouts it is under Settings, then Connectors.
connect.claude.s3: Name: CortexMind. Remote MCP server URL: paste your Public URL. Click Add.
connect.claude.s4: Click Connect next to CortexMind. A CortexMind sign-in page opens: paste your CortexMind Password (the field may be labeled Bearer Token) and click Authorize.
connect.claude.s5: Teach it the habit: in Settings, find the instructions Claude keeps for every chat (“Instructions for Claude”, or “What personal preferences should Claude consider in responses?”). Paste the AI Instructions from CortexMind's Settings and save.
connect.claude.s6: Test it: start a new chat, click + at the bottom left, open Connectors and make sure CortexMind is on. Ask “What do you know about me?” and allow CortexMind when Claude asks. Choose “Always allow” to skip the question next time.
connect.trouble.title: If something does not work
connect.trouble.a1: Check that CortexMind says Running in your menu bar or tray. After a restart, give it a minute, then try again. Make sure you pasted the Public URL, not the Local URL.
connect.trouble.q2: It asks for a password and refuses mine.
connect.trouble.a2: Copy the CortexMind Password again from CortexMind's Settings. It is not your license key and not your ChatGPT or Claude password.
connect.trouble.q3: It answers, but never uses my memory.
connect.trouble.a3: Start a new chat, check that the connector is turned on for it, and check that the AI Instructions are saved in your custom instructions. Without them, the AI only uses its memory when it feels like it.
connect.trouble.q4: It worked yesterday and stopped today.
connect.trouble.a4: Your computer is probably asleep or CortexMind is not running. Wake it up, wait until the icon says Running, then start a new chat.
connect.agents: Using Claude Code, Codex or Cursor instead? Those run on your computer and connect differently: see the setup guide.
